drivers.why: An electric car uses several times the copper of a petrol car; solar, wind and data centres add to this newer demand.
China uses about half of the world's copper. Its property market and factory data move the price.
Chile, Peru and Congo produce much of the world's copper; strikes, floods and new rules at big mines can cut supply quickly.
Copper is often called 'Dr Copper' because it tends to fall when traders expect a slowdown; trade tariffs also move it.

drivers.why: Gold pays no interest, so when US rates after inflation rise, holding it costs more and the price has tended to fall; when they drop, it has tended to rise.
Gold is priced in dollars. A stronger dollar usually means a lower dollar gold price, and the other way round.
Central banks (China, India, Poland, Turkey and others) have bought heavily since 2022, a large source of demand.
War, bank failures and market crashes send money to gold as a store of value; calm periods can do the opposite.
For an Indian buyer the rupee matters as much as the metal: a weaker rupee lifts the rupee price even if the dollar price is flat.
Weddings, Dhanteras, Diwali and Akshaya Tritiya bring seasonal buying; import duty changes in the Budget move local prices overnight.

drivers.why: About half of silver is used by industry: solar panels, electronics, electric cars. Factory activity matters more than for gold.
Silver usually moves the same way as gold but by more, both up and down, because its market is much smaller.
Most silver is mined as a by-product of copper, lead and zinc, so supply barely reacts to the silver price itself.
How many ounces of silver buy one ounce of gold; this page's top section shows where it stands against its history.
Like gold, the rupee price also depends on USD/INR and on India's import duty and 3% GST.
